name: Enlightened absolutism
summary: Enlightened absolutism is the eighteenth-century idea that an absolute monarch should use reason, science and reform to improve his subjects' welfare while keeping all political power. The ruler is the first servant of the state, but subjects are not partners in government: everything for the people, nothing by the people.
scope: Mainstream of the eighteenth-century European strand: Frederick II of Prussia, Catherine II of Russia, Joseph II and Charles III, with Frederick's essay as the primary text. Excludes modern uses of the label for authoritarian modernizers.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Rulers eased trade and followed Physiocrat ideas in places, yet kept guild, tariff and state-directed economic policy under Cameralism.

public-ownership.rationale: Monarchs owned royal manufactories and domains but did not advocate public ownership of industry as a principle; adherents split by policy.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Joseph II pushed a more equitable tax burden including nobles, and rulers overrode noble tax exemptions to fund the state.

property-fundamental.rationale: Rulers dissolved monasteries and seized church assets and overrode noble privileges when state reform demanded it, so property was subordinate to state aims.

worker-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the doctrine envisages workers owning enterprises; power and ownership stayed with crown and elites.

strong-leader.rationale: The whole doctrine rests on a monarch who reforms from above without sharing power, unimpeded by estates or parliaments.

state-harmful.rationale: The doctrine exists to strengthen the state as an instrument of reform and welfare; Frederick calls the sovereign the state's chief servant.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

reviewHistory.rationale: Frederick's Prussia built its army and the ruler acted as chief general; police administration was central to Cameralist states.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not a doctrinal issue; Enlightenment rulers' practice varied widely.

decide-locally.rationale: Joseph II issued thousands of edicts for a uniform centrally run state and sidelined local diets such as Hungary's.

rehabilitation.rationale: Catherine's Instruction drew on Beccaria to condemn torture and cruel punishment, and Joseph II's code stressed prison labor over executions.

more-religion-public.rationale: Rulers curbed church power, closed monasteries and put clergy under state control, though they kept established churches.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Rulers such as Joseph II imposed German as the official language over local traditions, while others promoted national institutions; no common line.

gradual-change.rationale: Enlightened absolutists imposed rapid reform from above, as Joseph II's flood of edicts shows, overriding established institutions, though they kept the monarchy.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: International organizations did not exist; rulers prized sovereign state power.

free-trade.rationale: Charles III eased trade but Cameralist states kept protective policies; split.

nation-first.rationale: Rulers pursued state strength and interest, as Frederick did, though Enlightenment cosmopolitanism complicated this.

open-borders.rationale: Rulers controlled borders and subjects through the state; open borders is far from the doctrine.

limit-growth.rationale: Rulers sought growing revenue, population and trade; limiting growth contradicts this.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Rulers promoted science, universities, statistics and agricultural improvement as tools of progress.

revolution-justified.rationale: Reform is imposed from above to preserve absolute rule; subjects have no political role and revolts against Joseph II's reforms were put down.

land-value-tax.rationale: The Physiocrats proposed a single land tax and influenced some rulers, but adoption varied.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Cameralist and mercantilist states generally protected domestic manufactures, though Physiocrat influence cut against it.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Rulers founded manufactories, promoted agriculture and trade, and used statistics for long-term planning.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Peasant emancipation moved toward small farmers in places, but nothing on property distribution was doctrine.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Contrary to the era's state-led commerce and tax finance.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Rulers reduced the privileges of estates and guilds in favor of direct state authority; wage setting by bodies is not a theme.

one-party-rule.rationale: The model is rule by the monarch, not a party; party politics is absent.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The doctrine is a defense of hereditary monarchy at its best; Frederick argues monarchy can surpass republics given an active, honest sovereign.

democracy-best.rationale: Subjects had no role in politics and the motto was everything for the people, nothing by the people.

direct-votes.rationale: Enlightened monarchs sidelined even representative bodies such as the Hungarian Diet, so direct popular votes on laws had no place.

workers-councils.rationale: Political power rests with the crown, not any popular bodies.

right-to-secede.rationale: Rulers built uniform centralized states and Joseph II abolished separate administrations.

natural-rulers.rationale: Frederick holds that an able, hard-working sovereign is the head of the political body, yet legitimacy was dynastic and he held the ruler's duties, not innate rank, central.

political-violence-never.rationale: Rulers used force at home and abroad but rejected popular violence; the statement is ambiguous for this stance.

war-builds-character.rationale: Charles III sought to avoid war and Enlightenment thinkers distrusted it, though Frederick waged many; split but leaning no.

separate-church-state.rationale: Rulers subordinated the church to the state rather than separating them; Joseph II placed clergy under state control.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Law was reformed by reason and rulers' codification, as Catherine drew on Montesquieu and Beccaria.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The ruler is chief judge and general; justice and arms are state functions.

military-superiority.rationale: Frederick's Prussia built the state around military might and the ruler is chief general.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Multiethnic dynastic empires were the setting; Joseph II ruled many peoples, though he imposed German.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The crown stands above estates and promotes unity; Frederick says ruler and people are one body.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Reforms sought legal equality at best, not equal outcomes.

civilizational-union.rationale: Dynastic state interest was the focus; religion-based union not a theme.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The ruler's duty is service to the state, and morals and education of subjects are state goals.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Subjects had no political role and owed duties to the state, while the sovereign too was its servant; rights were granted from above.

limit-population.rationale: Cameralism favored larger populations as a source of state strength.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Rulers pushed science and modernization from above, though they preserved their own institutions.

restore-past-order.rationale: Rulers attacked old privileges and church power in the name of progress and enlightenment.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Reform was justified by welfare and efficiency of the state, but the monarchy itself was not up for assessment.

direct-action.rationale: Change comes from the throne, not from popular action.

means-match-ends.rationale: Rulers used authoritarian means for liberal-sounding ends, as with Joseph II legislating by edict.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Directly opposed to progress and improvement.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not part of any enlightened-absolutist outlook.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Rulers provided welfare but not distribution by need as a principle.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not a notion of the doctrine.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The crown's rule stands above classes.

collective-farming.rationale: Rulers modernized agriculture and freed peasants, not collectivized farms.

taxation-theft.rationale: Frederick criticizes wasteful use of taxes by rulers but treats taxation as the lawful basis of state service.

harm-principle.rationale: Rulers regulated religion, education and morals paternally, though some toleration measures widened liberty.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rights were granted by the sovereign; legal equality was a goal but not natural rights against the crown.

conscription.rationale: Absolutist states like Prussia built armies through compulsory service systems; the state's call on subjects was accepted.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Subjects have neither a vote nor an institutional check; rulers kept the right to bind subjects.

state-as-business.rationale: The ruler is servant of the state and head of one body with the people, not a business provider to customers.

media-academia-power.rationale: Rulers hired philosophers as advisers yet controlled them and censored where needed.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; Enlightenment universalism pulls against it.

organic-representation.rationale: Rulers cut the power of estates and corporate bodies in favor of direct crown authority.

total-state.rationale: Rulers regulated economy, education and church widely, but not every area as an aim; some freedom of thought was allowed.

national-rebirth.rationale: Reform and improvement, not decadence and rebirth, is the framing.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Frederick and Catherine expanded their realms, though Charles III sought to avoid war; split among rulers.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rulers replaced feudal ties with a bureaucratic central state and rational administration.

bound-labor.rationale: Joseph II abolished serfdom while Catherine II kept and extended it, so the rulers split.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The doctrine rests on Enlightenment confidence that reason finds objective truth to combat ignorance and prejudice.

universal-morality.rationale: Enlightenment rulers appealed to reason and natural law, as in Catherine's use of Montesquieu and Beccaria for universal principles.

single-common-good.rationale: Catherine held that absolute rule directs everyone toward the common good, and Frederick describes the ruler as embodying the interest of the whole state.

revive-national-language.rationale: Joseph II imposed a single official language rather than reviving old ones.

workplace-democracy.rationale: No role for democratic governance anywhere in the doctrine.

school-vouchers.rationale: Rulers created state-controlled standard school systems, as Joseph II's 1774 school ordinance did.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Frederick condemns wasting taxes and expects the sovereign to know and manage the state's finances; Joseph II reformed accounting.

economic-freedom.rationale: Political freedom was not what the doctrine sought; rulers kept political power regardless of economic liberalization.

rule-by-example.rationale: Frederick says rulers should be guardians of law and improve morals through example and avoid bad example.

national-self-determination.rationale: Multiethnic dynastic states denied it; Joseph II centralized over Hungarian objections.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Frederick says his chief task is to combat ignorance and prejudice, and rulers curbed church power in the name of reason.

class-collaboration.rationale: The sovereign and people form one body, firmly united, according to Frederick.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Rulers founded libraries, universities and museums.

ban-interest.rationale: Rulers promoted commerce and credit; usury bans were being abandoned.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; legal equality was the aim, and Joseph II eased restrictions on Jews.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The doctrine presents the crown as above classes and serving the whole people, and often fighting noble privilege.

proportional-representation.rationale: No elected legislature of any kind is part of the system.

national-mission.rationale: Enlightened monarchs reformed their own realms rather than export governments.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Rulers did not treat gender relations as a structural problem.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Frederick blames bad government on a ruler's character and favourites, so corruption is dealt with by good sovereigns, not distrust of the system.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The ruler is chief general and judge; Frederick expects accountability only to citizens in principle.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The ruler is active in economy, education, morals and religion, so a minimal state is rejected.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Catherine's Instruction proclaimed equality of all before the law, and Joseph II aimed at legal equality of classes, though both kept serfdom or ranks in practice.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Rulers codified and unified laws and aimed at legal equality across classes; Joseph II issued thousands of laws.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Toleration reforms eased restrictions but established churches were kept; split.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: State schools were often run with clerical involvement; rulers controlled but did not ban religion in education.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Subjects had no political role, and Joseph II felt he could speak for the state without being bound by laws or diets.

trade-surplus.rationale: Cameralist and mercantilist policy sought export surpluses to enrich the state.

population-transfer.rationale: Rulers resettled populations and colonists in places, but no principle of expelling minorities.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Progress is driven by the enlightened ruler from above, not by struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: No parties existed; the regime banned opposition by default.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The subject depends on the sovereign's goodwill, the very arbitrary power this statement opposes; the ruler was not bound by law.

separated-powers.rationale: Frederick's sovereign is chief judge, general, financier and minister at once, and Joseph II sidelined the diet.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Rulers aimed at the welfare of all subjects, not any priority.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Cameralists favored population growth though Malthus came later.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices were filled by royal appointment of capable officials.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Cameralist states regulated grain markets in scarcity, though Physiocrat influence cut the other way.

party-controls-media.rationale: No party exists; rulers did censor, though Joseph II relaxed it.

party-commands-army.rationale: The ruler himself commands, as Frederick's role as chief general shows.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Rulers guarded sovereignty and centralized authority.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The monarch is chief general and appoints his ministers; Frederick lists these among the sovereign's duties.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Rulers subordinated the church to the crown whatever its internal form was.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rulers took power from the church, closed monasteries and put clergy under state control.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; subjects owe loyalty to the sovereign.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Rulers improved morals as a duty, but practice varied from French censorship to Joseph II's relaxed controls.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials answered to the crown, not voters.

people-in-arms.rationale: Rulers built professional standing armies under royal command.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Physiocrats praised agriculture, but rulers also built towns and manufactures.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Rulers relied on educated advisers and promoted universities.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Enlightenment rulers saw their own era's reason and progress as superior to prejudice and ignorance.

death-penalty.rationale: Catherine disapproved and Joseph II effectively abolished it, while others retained it; split.

minority-language-support.rationale: Joseph II made German compulsory for official business over resistance.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Rulers shaped subjects' morals and education from above; Frederick's sovereign improves morals.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Rulers issued their own legal codes from above and gave the people no role in framing them, which excludes an elected constituent assembly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The doctrine accepts curtailed political freedom while the ruler modernizes the state and economy.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state was a hereditary monarch, so a popularly elected head of state had no place.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Dynastic rulers traded territory in treaties as suited them.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Rulers overrode church and noble property when state welfare demanded, as in Joseph II's monastery dissolutions.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Frederick and Catherine annexed territory freely.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Joseph II dissolved monasteries and brought clergy under state control; Charles III also weakened the church.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Enlightened rulers justified power by reason and service to the state, not divine descent; Frederick II was a sceptic and Joseph II curbed the church.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The monarch kept all legislative power and was not accountable to subjects, though Frederick held he should rule by law for the state's good.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The defining formula is that the ruler keeps all political power, so sharing it with nobles or the people is rejected, though Frederick admired balanced constitutions in other states.

leader-cult.rationale: Rulers cultivated an image as benevolent reformers and accepted public honours, but Frederick disdained flattery; no clear doctrine either way.

land-redistribution.rationale: Rulers kept the nobility's estates while reforming serfdom from above, so wholesale seizure was not their policy.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Joseph II's toleration patents and Frederick's tolerance show a stance against punishing religious dissent.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Joseph II centralised and imposed German as an administrative language, against minority autonomy.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Reform comes from above by the ruler, with nothing by the people.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: They kept hereditary monarchy and largely preserved noble privilege, though Joseph II curbed some.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Colonial tutelage was not an enlightened-absolutist theme and the Enlightenment itself was split on empire; no clear inference.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The ruler keeps all power, and Frederick and Catherine ruled out limits on the sovereign; a charter that binds the crown is contrary to absolutism.

elective-rulers.rationale: Enlightened absolutism kept hereditary monarchy and denied subjects a share in choosing the ruler.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Subjects were to serve the state; the ruler was its first servant but accountable to no one, and the formula was everything for the people, nothing by the people.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The monarch kept all legislative power; representative bodies had no supremacy.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The rulers did not address animal sentience; Enlightenment opinion was divided, so no stable position is inferable.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The ruler as first servant of the state owed paternal care to subjects, shown in welfare, schooling and toleration reforms.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Catherine's Nakaz argued that Russia's size required autocracy, and Frederick's essay tied forms of government to circumstances.

office-by-exam.rationale: Frederick II and Joseph II staffed bureaucracies by merit and ability rather than election, with the ruler as first servant of the state.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Rule rested with the monarch, "everything for the people, nothing by the people", so leaders bound and removable by their electors had no place.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The monarch kept all political power and did not need parliamentary consent to spend, as the sources describe.

single-official-language.rationale: Joseph II imposed German as the administrative language across the Habsburg lands, and Catherine II promoted Russian state centralisation.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The subject owes obedience to the sovereign: reform comes from above and subjects are not partners in government.

religious-nation.rationale: Joseph II's toleration edicts and Frederick II's view that everyone may seek salvation his own way separate state membership from one religion.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Rulers like Joseph II centralized administration and finance under the crown, overriding provincial privileges, so regional revenue retention is disfavoured.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: These rulers protected private property and never proposed common ownership of land or tools; Joseph II's reforms freed peasants but kept private holdings.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

religion-illusion.rationale: Rulers like Frederick were sceptical of religion, yet Catherine and Joseph used it for social order; no consistent position on its fading.

treaties-binding.rationale: The sovereign stands above law, and Joseph II overrode traditional constitutions and privileges of Hungary and other lands when reform required.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Enlightened absolutists wanted a strong centralized state and rejected self-governing communes with common property.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Rulers reformed criminal law in a rationalist direction but the sources do not settle same-sex law; adherents split.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Joseph II's Toleration Patent and Frederick's essay favour toleration over punishing false religion.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Frederick's essay defends monarchy with a single ruler, and the rulers reserved decisions to themselves.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Frederick calls the ruler the first servant of the state, and authority rests on service and reason rather than God.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Frederick of Prussia built a large standing army and the rulers relied on military power.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Enlightened absolutists were hereditary monarchs who kept the crown within the dynasty, and none proposed electing the ruler.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Rulers issued codes and reforms, as Catherine's Nakaz urged legal order, yet kept the power to rule by decree, so adherents are split.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Joseph II's toleration measures and Catherine's rule favoured protection of religious minorities, not shunning them.

citizens-assembly.rationale: The motto is everything for the people, nothing by the people; the monarch decides on reason and advice from officials, so citizens sharing in decisions contradicts the doctrine.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Enlightened monarchs such as Joseph II subordinated churches to the state and promoted toleration and rational reform of religion, so they favoured updating over inherited church rulings.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Enlightened rulers curbed noble privileges but defended property and rank; the topic is hardly addressed and the label is split.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Enlightened rulers promoted religious toleration and reform, not atheism, and kept state churches; Joseph II reformed rather than abolished religion.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Enlightened rulers expanded state welfare and education as the monarch's duty to improve subjects' welfare; they did not rely on charity.

vote-delegation.rationale: Everything for the people, nothing by the people: subjects do not take part in government.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Loyalty was to the dynasty and the state, which Joseph II tried to unify across peoples, rather than to an ancient national identity.

culture-before-state.rationale: The state was the engine of reform in this strand, which acted from the top rather than waiting for cultural renewal.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Enlightened rulers were sceptical rationalists who tolerated religion and used it for social order, so the claim is neither endorsed nor rejected.

communal-electorates.rationale: Joseph II's reforms, such as the Edict of Tolerance, made all subjects answer to one state; separate communal representation did not exist and contradicts a unified sovereign.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Absolute monarchs held a monopoly of force through standing armies and police, with no armed bodies beyond the crown's control.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: War and the army served the monarch's state, as in Frederick's Prussia; soldiers refusing orders is incompatible with absolutism.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Enlightened absolutists sought to strengthen and rationalise the state machine, not destroy it.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The sovereign directed reform and the economy from above in one uniform system, as in Catherine's Nakaz.

sacred-nation.rationale: Loyalty was to the dynasty and state rather than a sacred nation; the nation as sacred community is a later idea, so adherents are split.

workers-own-party.rationale: The formula 'everything for the people, nothing by the people' excludes independent political organisation by subjects.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not an issue for the doctrine; language policy varied, so it is genuinely split.

voter-id.rationale: Rulers held absolute power with no elections, so the question has no application.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: The rationalist rulers subordinated the church and treated religion as a matter of utility and toleration, not literal revelation (Joseph II, Frederick).

national-church-status.rationale: Adherents differ: Joseph II granted toleration and curbed the church, while others kept established churches privileged.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Joseph II centralised the Habsburg lands and overrode local and national autonomies, as s4 describes.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Catherine's Nakaz rejected torture and argued for punishment by law, and Joseph II reformed criminal law; trial was part of reform.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Frederick's essay makes the sovereign the servant of the state with no partnership of subjects; the ruler governs without estates or factions.

missingStatements.text: A ruler should keep all political power while governing for the welfare of his subjects.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the defining formula: reforms for the people by an absolute ruler, with no sharing of power.

missingStatements.text: The state should reduce the power and property of the church and subordinate clergy to civil authority.
missingStatements.rationale: Joseph II dissolved monasteries and brought clergy under state control; Charles III also weakened the church.

notes: Scholars dispute whether the category is useful; Frederick held enlightened ideas privately but often did not enact reforms, and Catherine left serfdom intact while Joseph II abolished it.
